title: "Maps in RStudio"
format: html

ramb's map functions put your data on an interactive map in RStudio's
Viewer pane. You declare the map in R: its layers, how each is drawn,
and what a click shows. [rb_map_serve()](../reference/rb_map_serve.html)
then serves it from your R session, on your own computer only
(`127.0.0.1`). The data stay in DuckDB. As you pan and zoom, the page
asks for vector tiles, and DuckDB cuts each one from the table, so a
table of millions of rows draws as quickly as a small one. The page
([MapLibre GL JS](https://maplibre.org/)) does the colours, filters,
legends and popups. [rb_map_bundle()](../reference/rb_map_bundle.html)
writes the same map as a folder that opens from its `index.html`, with
no R and no server, to send to someone.

You need the httpuv and jsonlite packages
(`install.packages(c("httpuv", "jsonlite"))`) and DuckDB's spatial
extension, which ramb loads, and installs the first time, when it first
cuts a tile. The depth and relief need the png package too.

The examples use data shipped with ramb, read with
[rb_read_example()](../reference/rb_read_example.html): the Danish pings
(`dansk`, from [WKSSFGEO](https://github.com/ices-eg/WKSSFGEO)), the
harbours they come and go from (`dansk_harbours`) and the seabed under
them (`dansk_relief`, NOAA's ETOPO 2022). Run the chunks in
RStudio's console one by one. The chunks that build layers run as they
are; the chunks that serve a map open it in the Viewer pane.

## The quick look

To see pings at once, pipe them into
[rb_map_pings()](../reference/rb_map_pings.html), which draws them as
points coloured by a column (speed by default) on a dark base map, and
[rb_map_track()](../reference/rb_map_pings.html), which joins them into
each vessel's track. Each adds its layer to the map piped into it, and
the map opens in the Viewer when printed, so a chain shows once, at its
end:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ramb)
rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  rb_map_pings(time = "time_stamp")
rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  rb_map_track(behaviour, time = "time_stamp", by = vessel_id) |>
  rb_map_pings(c(behaviour, speed))
```

The second map's line is cut into runs of `behaviour` and coloured by it,
and its points can be coloured by either column, chosen under *Colour by*.
Grouped pings, `group_by(vessel_id)`, give the page a list of the groups
above the layers, to show one at a time, with buttons that step through
them.
A map printed replaces the one before it. The rest of this article builds
maps layer by layer, for when the quick look is not enough.

## Pings over time: a panel under the map

[rb_map_time()](../reference/rb_map_time.html) adds a panel under the map
that shows one vessel's pings over time: a column or several as lines
(speed by default), marks where a column says so, and lanes of intervals.
The panel and the map are linked:

- drag across the chart to choose a time, and the map shows that window's
  track and pings, and zooms to them; a double click, or *Whole span*,
  shows the whole span again;
- hover over the chart to see the ping on the map, and click a ping on the
  map to find its time on the chart;
- click an interval in a lane to set the window to it.

Here the panel draws the Danish pings' speed and course, with lanes for
the labelled behaviour and gear. The pings are read from their parquet
file as they are, with no copy into R, as in the quick look:

```{r}
library(ramb)

m <- rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  rb_map_track(
    behaviour,
    time = "time_stamp",
    by = vessel_id,
    title = "Danish pings over time"
  ) |>
  rb_map_time(
    c(speed, course),
    lanes = list(behaviour = "behaviour", gear = "gear")
  )
m
```

Printed at the console, the map opens in the Viewer pane (here, knitted,
it prints what it holds). The panel's controls are in the sidebar, under
*Time*: choose a vessel there, and the map shows only its pings. Its speed is drawn in blue on
the left axis; tick *course* to add it, on its own scale on the right.
The lanes under the chart are the runs of `behaviour` and `gear`, each
value in its own colour.

The track, the chart and the lanes join a vessel's pings however long it
falls silent, so no gap is hidden: a silence shows as a long straight
line. To break them where two pings are more than an hour apart, give
the track `max_gap_s = 3600` (in seconds); the panel takes the track's.

Some things to know:

- **Marks:** `marks =` names columns that mark pings, such as flags:
  each column a row of ticks along the chart's top and a ring on the map
  at each ping it marks (a logical column's `TRUE`s, any other's values
  that are not missing), in a colour of its own, named in the sidebar.
  `marks = c(truth = "wrong", clean = "flag")` names them.

- **The page holds one vessel at a time, its whole series by default:**
  raw pings need nothing more than a time and a position. To step through
  a vessel's trips, or any other intervals, name them in `span`: a column
  of the pings, `span = c(trip = "trip_id")`, or a table of intervals as
  for the lanes. The map then shows only the chosen trip. A vessel with
  more than `span_max` pings (3 million) is offered by its spans, else by
  month.
- **The map stays quick.** The window's track is drawn whole, and its
  pings are thinned to about 5,000 (every second, third, ... ping; a
  marked one always kept). The panel says when they are.
- **Times are shown as stored,** in no time zone. `time_label` names the
  clock beside them, UTC by default.
- **Lanes can be tables of intervals:** port calls from
  [rb_create_port_calls()](../reference/rb_create_port_calls.html),
  voyages from [rb_create_voyages()](../reference/rb_create_voyages.html),
  records' windows, or any table with the vessel column and a `start` and
  an `end`:

  ```{r}
  #| eval: false
  rb_map_time(pings, lanes = list(`port calls` = port_calls, voyages = voyages))
  ```
- **The vessel, the span and the window go into the address,** so a link
  opens the same view, and [rb_map_bundle()](../reference/rb_map_bundle.html)
  writes the panel's pings beside the page, so it works with no R and no
  server.

## A first map

A map is layers, in groups. Here is one layer, the harbours as polygons:

```{r}
library(ramb)

harbour_tiles <- rb_map_tiles_table(
  rb_read_example("dansk_harbours"),
  properties = "SI_HARB"
)

harbours <- rb_map_layer(
  "harbours", "vector",
  label = "Harbours",
  tiles = harbour_tiles,
  style = list(list(
    id = "harbours-fill", type = "fill", "source-layer" = "features",
    paint = list("fill-color" = "#d9822b", "fill-opacity" = 0.6)
  )),
  popup = list(click = "harbours-fill", title = "SI_HARB")
)

m <- rb_map(
  rb_map_group("ref", "Reference", list(harbours)),
  title = "Danish harbours",
  view = list(center = c(10.5, 56), zoom = 7)
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m)
```

The map opens in the Viewer pane. The sidebar lists the layers (tick a
layer to show it), with the base maps and a button that copies a link
to the view. Click a harbour for its id (`SI_HARB`). On a narrow pane the sidebar
sits behind a menu button. The Viewer's *Show in new window* button opens
the same page in your browser, where there is more room.

What each part does:

- [rb_map_tiles_table()](../reference/rb_map_tiles_table.html) copies the
  table once into a temporary DuckDB table, in web mercator, and returns
  the tile function the layer needs. Its features are in the tile layer
  `"features"`, which `style` names as its `"source-layer"`.
- `style` is a list of [MapLibre layer
  specifications](https://maplibre.org/maplibre-style-spec/layers/),
  written as R lists.
- `popup` names the styles that answer a click (`click`) and the field
  shown as the popup's title. Its `fields` add lines under the title; a
  field's `values` turn a code into a text
  (`values = list(F = "fishing")`), and its `template` writes the value
  into a sentence (`template = "{SI_HARB} of 942"`).
- **Small areas, zoomed out.** A harbour is a few pixels across at zoom
  7. `rb_map_tiles_table(..., points = "points")` adds a second tile
  layer, `"points"`, with a point on each feature, which a `circle`
  style with a `maxzoom` draws where the areas are too small to see.

A tile function can be called directly. That is a quick way to see that
a layer has something to show before you serve it:

```{r}
attr(harbour_tiles, "count") # the number of features
length(harbour_tiles(7, 68, 39)) # the bytes of one tile at zoom 7
```

## The map lives in your R session

The server runs in the background of the R session that started it,
which has some consequences:

- **It answers while the console is idle.** While R runs something else,
  the map waits: tiles stop arriving until the console is free.
- **Serving again replaces it.** Change the map and run
  `rb_map_serve(m)` again: the server on that port is stopped, a new one
  started, and the Viewer reloads.
- **Several maps need several ports.** For example,
  `rb_map_serve(m2, port = 8791)`. The default is 8790. If another
  program holds the port, you get an error that says so.
- **`rb_map_stop()` stops them.** With no argument it stops every map
  this session serves; `rb_map_stop(8791)` stops one. Restarting R stops
  them too, after which the Viewer shows a page with nothing behind it.
  Serve again.

## Points coloured by a value

The pings as points, coloured by the behaviour in the data or by their
speed, as the reader chooses. There are 395,558 of them. Drawn at a
zoomed-out view, nearly all would fall in a few tiles, each slow to cut
and send. `minzoom = 10` keeps the points to zoom 10 and closer; the
next section shows the pings as cells for the overview.

```{r}
by_behaviour <- list("match", list("get", "behaviour"), "Fishing", "#c0392b", "#8a959e")
by_speed <- list(
  "interpolate", list("linear"), list("get", "speed"),
  0, "#2166ac", 3, "#f4a582", 8, "#b2182b"
)

pings <- rb_map_layer(
  "pings", "vector",
  label = "Pings",
  info = "Each ping, coloured by the behaviour in the data or by its speed.",
  minzoom = 10,
  tiles = rb_map_tiles_table(
    rb_read_example("dansk"),
    lon = "lon", lat = "lat",
    properties = c("vessel_id", "time_stamp", "speed", "behaviour")
  ),
  count = list(text = "{1} pings"),
  style = list(list(
    id = "pings-dot", type = "circle", "source-layer" = "features",
    paint = list(
      "circle-color" = by_behaviour,
      "circle-radius" = list("interpolate", list("linear"), list("zoom"), 10, 2, 15, 5)
    )
  )),
  legend = list(
    list(swatch = list(dot = "#c0392b"), label = "fishing"),
    list(swatch = list(dot = "#8a959e"), label = "other")
  ),
  variants = list(
    label = "Colour by",
    options = list(
      list(
        value = "behaviour", label = "behaviour",
        paint = list("pings-dot" = list("circle-color" = by_behaviour))
      ),
      list(
        value = "speed", label = "speed",
        paint = list("pings-dot" = list("circle-color" = by_speed)),
        legend = list(
          list(swatch = list(dot = "#2166ac"), label = "0 knots"),
          list(swatch = list(dot = "#f4a582"), label = "3 knots"),
          list(swatch = list(dot = "#b2182b"), label = "8 knots or more")
        )
      )
    )
  ),
  popup = list(
    click = "pings-dot", title = "vessel_id",
    fields = list(
      list(field = "time_stamp", label = "time"),
      list(field = "speed", label = "speed (knots)", format = "value"),
      list(field = "behaviour", label = "behaviour")
    )
  )
)
```

Some things to note:

- **MapLibre's expressions are lists**, so that a one-element array such
  as `list("zoom")` stays an array when the map is sent to the page. Write
  `list("get", "behaviour")`, not `c("get", "behaviour")`.
- **A vector tile holds only text, numbers and logicals.** So
  `rb_map_tiles_table()` carries a date-time such as `time_stamp` as text,
  and a factor or a date too.
- **`count` puts the number of features beside the layer's label.**
- **`variants` are colourings to choose between**, under *Colour by*
  when the layer is ticked. Each option sets paint properties of the
  layer's styles, by style id, and may bring its own legend; the first
  is shown when the page opens. A choice changes the paint only: no tile
  is fetched again.

## Cells: a grid with filters

A grid layer is the main data layer of a map: cells coloured on a log
scale. The page adds the controls: the palette, how the colours stretch
over the values, a floor and a cap, the opacity, and a histogram of the
cells in view. Its filters become controls too, whose values reach your
tile function. You write that function, so you choose the cell and what
is summed in it. Here the pings are counted by 0.01-degree cell, with a
filter on behaviour:

```{r}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial") # the tiles are made with DuckDB's ST_ functions
dansk_sql <- dbplyr::sql_render(rb_read_example("dansk", con = con))

cell_tile <- function(z, x, y, params) {
  where <- if (is.null(params$behaviour)) {
    ""
  } else {
    sprintf("WHERE behaviour = %s", DBI::dbQuoteString(con, params$behaviour))
  }
  DBI::dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
    "WITH c AS (SELECT floor(lon * 100) AS cx, floor(lat * 100) AS cy, count(*) AS n
                FROM (%s) %s GROUP BY ALL),
          m AS (SELECT n, ST_Transform(ST_MakeEnvelope(cx / 100, cy / 100, (cx + 1) / 100, (cy + 1) / 100),
                                       'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:3857', always_xy := true) AS env FROM c)
     SELECT ST_AsMVT({'geometry': ST_AsMVTGeom(env, ST_Extent(ST_TileEnvelope(%d, %d, %d)), 4096, 64, true),
                      'n': n::INTEGER}, 'cells', 4096) AS tile FROM m",
    dansk_sql, where, z, x, y
  ))$tile[[1]]
}

cells <- rb_map_layer(
  "cells", "grid",
  label = "Pings by cell",
  info = "The number of pings in each 0.01-degree cell.",
  tiles = cell_tile,
  meta = list(options = list(behaviour = data.frame(value = c("Fishing", "Other")))),
  filters = list(
    list(
      id = "behaviour", label = "Behaviour",
      options = list(list(value = "", label = "all")), meta = TRUE
    ),
    list(id = "metric", type = "metric", label = "Metric")
  ),
  metrics = list(list(field = "n", label = "pings")),
  popup = list(fields = list(list(field = "n", label = "pings", format = "count")))
)
```

How the parts fit together:

- **`tiles`** is called with the tile's `z`, `x` and `y`, and `params`, the
  filters' values. It returns a tile of cells in the tile layer
  `"cells"`, made by DuckDB's `ST_AsMVT()`.
- **The `behaviour` filter** offers "all" (no value) and the options in
  `meta`.
- **The server checks every value** against the filter's options before
  the tile function sees it. So `params$behaviour` is either absent or
  one of `"Fishing"` and `"Other"`, and it is safe to put into the SQL.
- **`metrics` are the fields the cells can be coloured by.** The
  `"metric"` filter chooses among them.
- **A map has one grid at most.**

A filter can also have fixed options with a default (a choice of cell
size, say) or be a range of two values (the first and last year).
[rb_map_layer()](../reference/rb_map_layer.html) describes them. The
function above sums the whole table for every tile, which is fine for
the example. For a large table, sum it once into a table of cells and
cut the tiles from that.

The tile function can be tried before serving, as above:

```{r}
length(cell_tile(7, 68, 39, list())) # every ping
length(cell_tile(7, 68, 39, list(behaviour = "Fishing"))) # fishing only
```

## Lines: each vessel's day

Any table of geometries becomes a vector layer. Here the lines are made
in DuckDB, one per vessel and day, through the day's pings in time
order. The layer has two controls of its own, a list that leaves out
the days with few pings and a box for thicker lines:

```{r}
tracks <- dplyr::tbl(con, dplyr::sql(sprintf(
  "SELECT vessel_id, CAST(time_stamp AS DATE) AS day, count(*) AS pings,
          ST_MakeLine(list(ST_Point(lon, lat) ORDER BY time_stamp)) AS geometry
   FROM (%s) GROUP BY ALL HAVING count(*) > 1",
  dansk_sql
)))

days <- rb_map_layer(
  "days", "vector",
  label = "Daily tracks", visible = FALSE,
  tiles = rb_map_tiles_table(tracks, properties = c("vessel_id", "day", "pings")),
  count = list(text = "{1} vessel days"),
  style = list(list(
    id = "days-line", type = "line", "source-layer" = "features",
    filter = list(">=", list("get", "pings"), list("global-state", "days_least")),
    paint = list(
      "line-color" = "#2c5d87",
      "line-width" = list("case", list("global-state", "days_thick"), 3, 1.5),
      "line-opacity" = 0.7
    )
  )),
  state = list(
    list(
      id = "least", label = "Days with at least", default = 0,
      options = list(
        list(value = 0, label = "one ping"),
        list(value = 1000, label = "1,000 pings"),
        list(value = 5000, label = "5,000 pings")
      )
    ),
    list(id = "thick", label = "Thick lines", default = FALSE)
  ),
  legend = list(list(swatch = list(fill = "#2c5d87"), label = "a vessel's day")),
  popup = list(
    click = "days-line", title = "vessel_id",
    fields = list(
      list(field = "day", label = "day"),
      list(field = "pings", label = "pings", format = "count")
    )
  )
)
```

`state` holds values in the reader's hands, which the layer's style
reads as `list("global-state", "<layer>_<control>")`: here
`days_least` in the line's filter and `days_thick` in its width. A
control with `options` is a list to choose from; one with only a
`default` of `TRUE` or `FALSE` is a box to tick. A change applies at
once, with nothing fetched again, so a state can filter features,
recolour them or move the zoom where a style starts. Every control must
be read by a style, or the layer is refused.

## Features from R: a GeoJSON layer

A small sf object can go to the page whole, as GeoJSON, with no tiles.
Here it is a box around the Kattegat:

```{r}
kattegat <- sf::st_sf(
  name = "Kattegat",
  geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(
    c(xmin = 10.5, ymin = 56, xmax = 12.9, ymax = 57.8),
    crs = 4326
  ))
)

area <- rb_map_layer(
  "area", "geojson",
  label = "Kattegat",
  data = kattegat,
  style = list(list(
    id = "area-line", type = "line",
    paint = list("line-color" = "#333333", "line-width" = 2, "line-dasharray" = list(2, 2))
  ))
)
```

A GeoJSON layer's style has no `"source-layer"`: there are no tiles to
pick a layer from.

On a busy map, clicking each feature to learn its name is slow. A label
on hover shows a feature's `title` beside the pointer as it moves over
it: `popup = list(click = "area-fill", hover = TRUE, title = "name")`
(`TRUE` takes the styles of `click`; or name the styles to `hover`), with
`hover_fields = TRUE` for its `fields` too. Where features overlap, the
topmost speaks, as for a click.

## Depth, relief and contours from a grid

A grid of elevations, such as a clip of GEBCO or of NOAA's ETOPO, gives
three layers: the depth in colour, the relief shaded, and contour
lines. [rb_map_tiles_dem()](../reference/rb_map_tiles_dem.html) makes
their tiles from a table of `lon`, `lat` and `elevation` (negative below
sea level): images of the elevations, from which the page draws all
three. Here it is `dansk_relief`, the seabed and the land around the
Danish pings at 30 arc-seconds (about 500 by 900 m):

```{r}
relief_tiles <- rb_map_tiles_dem(rb_read_example("dansk_relief"))
attributes(relief_tiles)[c("bounds", "maxzoom", "count")]
```

The depth's colours can follow the view: as the map settles, the page
asks a function of the view's box for the floor and the cap of the
palette. Given the depths' quantiles in view too, it offers colours in
equal shares, each colour as many cells as the next. This one reads the
grid, held in R:

```{r}
grid <- dplyr::collect(rb_read_example("dansk_relief"))
depth_in_view <- function(west, south, east, north) {
  inside <- grid$lon >= west & grid$lon <= east & grid$lat >= south & grid$lat <= north
  d <- -grid$elevation[inside & grid$elevation < 0]
  if (length(d) < 25) {
    return(NULL) # no sea in view
  }
  q <- unname(stats::quantile(d, seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 25)))
  floor <- max(1, signif(q[1], 2))
  list(floor = floor, cap = max(floor * 1.5, signif(q[25], 2)), quantiles = q)
}
depth_in_view(10.5, 56, 12.9, 57.8)[c("floor", "cap")] # the Kattegat
```

The three layers, all on the same tiles:

```{r}
depth <- rb_map_layer(
  "depth", "dem",
  label = "Depth",
  tiles = relief_tiles,
  style = list(list(id = "depth-colour", type = "color-relief")),
  colour = list(palette = "deep", scale = "equal", fit = depth_in_view)
)

relief <- rb_map_layer(
  "relief", "dem",
  label = "Relief",
  tiles = relief_tiles,
  style = list(list(id = "relief-shade", type = "hillshade")),
  shade = list(exaggeration = 0.6, shadow = "#1b2a3a")
)

major <- list("==", list("get", "level"), 1)
at_sea <- list(">", list("get", "ele"), 0)
contours <- rb_map_layer(
  "contours", "contour",
  label = "Depth contours",
  tiles = relief_tiles,
  contours = list(
    multiplier = -1, # depths, not elevations
    thresholds = list("5" = c(50, 100), "8" = c(10, 50), "10" = c(5, 25)),
    fit = depth_in_view
  ),
  style = list(
    list(
      id = "contours-line", type = "line", "source-layer" = "contours",
      filter = at_sea,
      paint = list("line-color" = "#1b2a3a", "line-width" = list("case", major, 1.2, 0.5))
    ),
    list(
      id = "contours-label", type = "symbol", "source-layer" = "contours",
      filter = list("all", at_sea, major),
      layout = list(
        "symbol-placement" = "line", "text-size" = 13,
        "text-field" = list("concat", list("to-string", list("get", "ele")), " m")
      ),
      paint = list("text-color" = "#1b2a3a")
    )
  ),
  legend = list(
    list(swatch = list(fill = "#1b2a3a"), label = "contour, labelled")
  )
)

m_seabed <- rb_map(
  rb_map_group("seabed", "Seabed", list(depth, relief, contours)),
  rb_map_group("ref", "Reference", list(harbours), open = FALSE),
  title = "The seabed around Denmark",
  view = list(center = c(10.5, 56.8), zoom = 6)
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m_seabed)
```

Each layer's controls appear under it when it is ticked: the depth's
palette, floor and cap, scale (log, linear or equal shares), ramp or
bands, a cut of the shallow end and opacity, with *Fit to view*; the
relief's light, its direction and height, intensity, opacity and
colours; and whether the contours follow the view. Some things to
know:

- **One grid, three layers.** The relief, the colours and the contours
  are drawn in the page from the same images, and a bundle writes them
  once.
- **The depth is the elevation's negative**, and what is 0 or less is
  left clear, so the land shows the base map. Turn `colour$of` to
  `"elevation"` for a map of the land. The relief is shaded on land and
  sea alike.
- **Equal shares part a plateau.** On a log scale a wide plateau at
  40-75 m takes one or two of the palette's steps and reads as one tone;
  in equal shares its channels and rim stand apart. `scale = "equal"`
  needs a `fit` that gives the quantiles.
- **The contours' `ele` is the depth** (`multiplier = -1`), and `level`
  is 1 on the major lines. The `thresholds` are the minor and major
  intervals from each zoom on; while the contours follow the view
  (the `fit`), the page puts about a dozen levels at round depths near
  the view's quantiles instead. The lines are made in the browser by
  [maplibre-contour](https://github.com/onthegomap/maplibre-contour),
  loaded only for a map that has a contour layer.
- **The shading's intensity can follow the view too:**
  `shade = list(fit = f)`, with `f` returning
  `list(exaggeration = )`, from 0 to 1.
- **Your own grid.** Any regular grid of longitude, latitude and
  elevation will do, as a data frame or a lazy table. marmap reads
  NOAA's:

  ```{r}
  #| eval: false
  b <- marmap::getNOAA.bathy(lon1 = 8, lon2 = 13, lat1 = 54.5, lat2 = 58, resolution = 1)
  own_tiles <- rb_map_tiles_dem(marmap::as.xyz(b), lon = "V1", lat = "V2", elevation = "V3")
  ```

  marmap labels the cells from the box's edge to its edge, up to half a
  cell from their centres; `data-raw/dansk_relief.R` in ramb's
  repository places them at their centres. A tile file you already have
  (MBTiles) is read with
  [rb_map_tiles_mbtiles()](../reference/rb_map_tiles_mbtiles.html).
- **Tiles are made as the page asks**, in a tenth of a second or two.
  Beyond `maxzoom` the map draws the deepest tiles enlarged.
- **The grid's edge reads as a coast.** Beyond its edge the tiles hold
  `nodata`, sea level by default, so where the grid ends in deep water
  the contours crowd along the edge and the relief shades a step there.
  Take a grid somewhat larger than the area you mean to show.

## All together, in two languages

The layers go into groups, and the groups into the map. Within a group,
a later layer is drawn over an earlier one. A group can start folded
(`open = FALSE`). Each text in the map (a title, label or info) is
looked up in `texts`, so it can be given in several languages. The page
then shows a language button for each, and its own texts stay English
unless you give them under the same keys. `locales` writes the numbers
in each language's manner, and `about` names the texts of an *About*
group.

The map also offers one vessel at a time, over the layers that carry
`vessel_id` (`choose`): a list above the groups, with buttons that step
through it. A choice shows only that vessel's pings and days and fits
the view to its `bbox`. The grid is summed by its tile function, so it
stays whole: a choice meant to reach it is a filter of its own.

```{r}
vessels <- rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(), lon0 = min(lon), lat0 = min(lat), lon1 = max(lon), lat1 = max(lat),
    .by = vessel_id
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(vessel_id) |>
  dplyr::collect()

one_vessel <- list(fields = list(list(
  field = "vessel_id",
  label = "Vessel",
  options = lapply(seq_len(nrow(vessels)), function(i) {
    list(
      value = vessels$vessel_id[i],
      label = sprintf("%s (%s pings)", vessels$vessel_id[i], format(vessels$n[i], big.mark = ",")),
      match = vessels$vessel_id[i],
      bbox = c(vessels$lon0[i], vessels$lat0[i], vessels$lon1[i], vessels$lat1[i])
    )
  }),
  layers = list("pings", "days")
)))

m <- rb_map(
  rb_map_group("data", "Data", list(cells, days, pings)),
  rb_map_group("ref", "Reference", list(harbours, area), open = FALSE),
  title = "Danish pings",
  view = list(center = c(10.5, 56.8), zoom = 6),
  texts = list(
    "Danish pings" = list(en = "Danish pings", da = "Danske positioner"),
    "Data" = list(en = "Data", da = "Data"),
    "Pings by cell" = list(en = "Pings by cell", da = "Positioner pr. celle"),
    "Daily tracks" = list(en = "Daily tracks", da = "Daglige spor"),
    "Pings" = list(en = "Pings", da = "Positioner"),
    "Behaviour" = list(en = "Behaviour", da = "Adfærd"),
    "Reference" = list(en = "Reference", da = "Reference"),
    "Harbours" = list(en = "Harbours", da = "Havne"),
    "Vessel" = list(en = "Vessel", da = "Fartøj"),
    about_data = list(
      en = "AIS positions of 14 Danish fishing vessels, 2012-2020, from the ICES workshop WKSSFGEO.",
      da = "AIS-positioner fra 14 danske fiskefartøjer, 2012-2020, fra ICES-workshoppen WKSSFGEO."
    )
  ),
  languages = c("en", "da"),
  locales = list(da = "da-DK"),
  about = "about_data",
  choose = one_vessel
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m)
```

The pings lie in a few patches: off Gothenburg, north of Jutland, in
the Øresund and south of Zealand. Zoom in on one past 10 and the points
appear over the cells. Tick *Daily tracks*
to see the vessels' days, and switch *Behaviour* to *Fishing* to see only
the cells of fishing pings. Choose a vessel above the groups, and the
pings and days are its own.

## The address is the view

Every choice in the page goes into its address, and the position
(zoom, latitude, longitude) after the `#`. The sidebar's link button
copies it. Opened again while the map is served, the link gives the same
view, so a view can be kept or sent to someone at the same computer.

`query` sets the first view from R. Each layer is a key (`1` on, `0`
off), as is each of the grid's filters, along with `metric`, `palette`,
`stretch` (`"even"` or `"equal"`), `floor` and `cap`, `opacity`, `base`
and `lang`. A layer's own controls are keys named after it: its colouring
`<layer>_by` (`pings_by`), each of its `state` controls
`<layer>_<control>` (`days_least`, `days_thick`), and a dem layer's
colours and shading, such as `depth_pal`, `depth_lo` and `depth_hi`
([rb_map_layer()](../reference/rb_map_layer.html) lists them). A
`choose` field is a key by its own name, several values separated by
commas:

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m, query = list(
  lang = "da", behaviour = "Fishing", palette = "viridis",
  base = "ocean", days = 1, days_least = 1000,
  pings_by = "speed", vessel_id = "EX_1"
))
```

The palettes and base maps to choose from:

```{r}
vapply(rb_map_palettes(), `[[`, "", "id")
vapply(rb_map_basemaps(), `[[`, "", "id")
```

## Notes on the map

A map served with a file for notes takes them from its reader: in the
Notes group, *Add a note*, a click on the map, a few words, and the
server writes the note to the file with the features under it and the
page's address. A reply joins a note's thread, from the page or from R,
so a map can carry a conversation about places: a red pin waits for an
answer, a blue one has one.

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m, notes = "danish_notes.geojson")
# later, in this R session or another
rb_map_notes("danish_notes.geojson")
rb_map_notes_add("danish_notes.geojson", "That patch is a mussel ground.", reply_to = 1)
```

The file is plain GeoJSON, a note a line, and opens in any GIS. A bundle
(`rb_map_bundle()`) has no server, and no notes.

## Verdicts: a question on each feature

A review goes faster where the features are seen. A layer's popup can
ask its reader questions about each feature, a button for each answer,
and a map served with a file for verdicts keeps the answers. Here each
harbour is asked whether it is one, and if it is, whether its outline
is right:

```{r}
review <- rb_map_layer(
  "harbours", "vector",
  label = "Harbours to check",
  tiles = harbour_tiles,
  style = list(list(
    id = "harbours-fill", type = "fill", "source-layer" = "features",
    paint = list("fill-color" = "#d9822b", "fill-opacity" = 0.6)
  )),
  popup = list(
    click = "harbours-fill",
    title = "SI_HARB",
    verdict = list(
      field = "SI_HARB",
      text = TRUE,
      questions = list(
        list(id = "harbour", label = "Is this a harbour?", options = list(
          list(value = "yes", label = "yes"),
          list(value = "no", label = "no")
        )),
        list(id = "outline", label = "Is its outline right?", skip = list(harbour = "no"), options = list(
          list(value = "right", label = "right"),
          list(value = "too_small", label = "too small"),
          list(value = "too_big", label = "too big")
        ))
      )
    )
  )
)

m_review <- rb_map(
  rb_map_group("review", "Review", list(review)),
  title = "Danish harbours, checked",
  view = list(center = c(10.5, 56), zoom = 7)
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
rb_map_serve(m_review, verdicts = "harbour_verdicts.csv")
# later, in this R session or another: each harbour's latest answer to each question
rb_map_verdicts("harbour_verdicts.csv")
```

Some things to know:

- **A verdict belongs to the feature's value of `field`**, here
  `SI_HARB`, so it is found again whichever tile the feature is drawn
  in. Each answer is written to the file with when, the place and the
  zoom; a later answer replaces the earlier, and
  `rb_map_verdicts(all = TRUE)` gives them all in the order given.
- **A mark on each feature judged**: the first question's answer is its
  fill, the second's its ring. The first option is green and the others
  red unless an option gives its own `colour`.
- **`skip`** leaves a question out after an earlier answer: here no
  outline is asked of a harbour that is not one. **`text = TRUE`** adds a
  note in the reader's own words.
- **An answer can name another feature** (`other = TRUE` on an option):
  a box for its name, the names in view offered.
- **Two layers of one kind of feature share answers** with `store`, the
  id of the layer that keeps them, so a feature's answer is the same
  whichever layer it is clicked on.
- As the notes, the verdicts are taken only from a page opened on this
  computer, and a bundle has none.

## A map in a folder

[rb_map_bundle()](../reference/rb_map_bundle.html) writes a map as a
folder whose `index.html` opens in a browser with a double click, on any
system, with no R and no server; it needs the internet only for MapLibre
and the base maps. The page, the layers' tiles and data are written
beside it as script files. A grid's tiles are made by a tile function
in R, so a bundle carries its rows instead, summed by cell at a few cell
sizes (`levels`), and the page makes the tiles from them, its filters
applied, as the server would. Here the cells and the seabed together:

```{r}
cell_rows <- rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  dplyr::mutate(x = floor(lon * 100), y = floor(lat * 100)) |>
  dplyr::count(x, y, behaviour)

m_folder <- rb_map(
  rb_map_group("data", "Data", list(cells)),
  rb_map_group("seabed", "Seabed", list(depth, relief, contours)),
  title = "Danish pings and the seabed",
  view = list(center = c(10.5, 56.8), zoom = 6)
)

folder <- rb_map_bundle(
  m_folder,
  file.path(tempdir(), "danish_pings"),
  maxzoom = 7,
  grids = list(cells = list(
    rows = cell_rows,
    unit = 0.01, # x and y count cells of 0.01 degrees
    levels = c(1, 2, 5, 10), # cells of 0.01, 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1 degrees
    columns = c(behaviour = "behaviour"), # the filter and its column
    sums = "n",
    fields = list(n = "n")
  )),
  overwrite = TRUE
)
c(tiles = attr(folder, "tiles"), megabytes = round(attr(folder, "bytes") / 1e6, 1))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
utils::browseURL(file.path(folder, "index.html"))
```

Some things to know:

- **What it carries**: geojson layers' data; the tiles of dem and
  contour layers to `maxzoom` inside their bounds; the tiles of
  [rb_map_tiles_table()](../reference/rb_map_tiles_table.html) layers
  that hold a feature; a time panel's
  spans; and the grids named in `grids`. Another vector layer is left
  out, with a message: its tiles are made by a server.
- **Each layer's `fit` is made in the browser**, from the tiles in view,
  by the rules in `rb_map_bundle(fit = )`, as no R is there to ask.
- **The deeper the zooms, the bigger the folder.** Past `maxzoom` the
  map draws the deepest tiles enlarged.
- No notes and no verdicts: they need the server.

## When a layer stays empty

- **Call its tile function** at a tile you know has data, as in the
  examples above. A tile of length zero has no features there.
- **A tile function's error shows in the page**, in the status line at
  the foot of the sidebar: the error's first line, for example a column
  that does not exist. The page shows it there because the console does
  not.
- **A vector layer with `minzoom` draws nothing** until you zoom in that
  far.
- **A dem layer's tile is an image.** `png::readPNG(relief_tiles(7, 67, 39))`
  gives its pixels; the elevation is red × 256 + green + blue / 256 −
  32768, each channel 0-255.

## More examples

Five whole maps on the example data come with ramb as scripts:

- the pings by cell (`dansk_map.R`);
- the same with a cell size, a sample and an interpolation to choose in
  the page (`dansk_switches_map.R`);
- the pings with a time panel under the map (`dansk_time_map.R`, the
  example above);
- the Italian tracks' voyages by two rules (`cnr_map.R`);
- the vessel in iapesca's example data (`iapesca_map.R`, which needs the
  iapesca package).

Copy one into your project to open it in RStudio and change it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
list.files(system.file("examples", "map", package = "ramb"))
file.copy(system.file("examples", "map", "cnr_map.R", package = "ramb"), ".")
file.edit("cnr_map.R")
```
